data.title: US hiring blows past forecasts as unemployment falls to 4.1%
data.description:
WASHINGTON – US job growth exceeded expectations in October, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, signalling a resilient labour market and giving the Federal Reserve greater scope to tackle inflation fuelled by the Middle East conflict.

Payrolls jumped by 165,000 jobs in October after an upwardly revised 60,000 gain in September, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labour Statistics said on Nov 6.

Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls advancing 65,000 after a previously reported 29,000 increase in September.

Estimates ranged from 35,000 to 125,000 jobs.

Economists estimated the US economy needs to create at least 40,000 jobs per month to keep up with growth in the working-age population. The so-called break-even rate has declined from roughly 150,000 in 2024 because of the smaller labour force.

The unemployment rate declined from 4.2% in September.

Professional and business services led the gains, adding 70,000 jobs, far above the sector’s average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past year.

Health care added 42,000 jobs, above its average monthly gain of 31,000 over the last year.

The sector has propped up the labour market in the United States in the last year, as an ageing population requires more care both in hospitals and at home.

Transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, mostly among couriers and messengers, while manufacturing added 19,000 jobs, the data showed.

Employment in other major sectors, including construction, retail, financial activities and government, was largely unchanged.

Average hourly earnings for all employees were up 3.1% over the past 12 months, with wages continuing to lag behind stubbornly high inflation, meaning most workers are seeing real wage losses.

Historically low layoffs and a recent jump in job openings have raised the prospect of labour market tightening.

But economists and US central bank officials have maintained that the labour market poses no inflation risk.

Some economists have argued that a shrinking supply of workers amid an immigration crackdown and retirements is the primary driver of the relatively low unemployment rate.

The Fed last week left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75% to 4% range. Economists expect a rate hike in December. The consumer inflation report for October due out on Nov 10 could offer more clues on the course of monetary policy in early 2027.

Despite the labour market resilience, job gains are lagging economic growth.

Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4% annualised rate in the third quarter, fuelled by strong consumer spending and businesses aggressively investing in artificial intelligence.

Economists said employers likely overhired after the Covid-19 pandemic, and some businesses were probably uncertain about their staffing needs as they incorporated AI into their operations.

They said uncertainty stemming from the US-Israel war with Iran, which has raised energy prices, is also making employers hesitant to increase headcount.

Limited opportunities have made it difficult for young adults, recent college graduates and some unemployed people to find work.

Disenchantment over the economy, as well as anger over the Middle East conflict, now in its ninth month, cost President Donald Trump’s Republican Party control of Congress, with Democrats performing strongly in this week’s midterm elections. REUTERS, AFP

data.title: Hong Kong economy’s surprise jump takes growth to five-year high
data.description:
HONG KONG – Hong Kong’s economy unexpectedly grew at a faster rate in the third quarter, taking expansion in the first nine months to the quickest in five years, thanks to a surge in exports and improved investment.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 5.2% from a year earlier, compared with a downwardly revised gain of 4.2% in the second quarter, according to advance estimates released on Nov 3 by the Census and Statistics Department.

Over the first nine months of 2026, GDP grew 5.1% from the same period in 2025. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, the economy also exceeded forecasts and expanded 1.9%.

“Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s economic outlook remains positive, with incoming data pointing to sustained growth momentum,” a government spokesman said in a statement, citing continued global investment in artificial intelligence and sustained growth in tourism among reasons for optimism.

A surge in exports, powered by strong global demand for electronics amid the AI supercycle, has been a key driver of growth for the transshipment hub and gateway to China.

Consumption and investment have also held up as the property market rebounds and infrastructure development for the Northern Metropolis gathers pace.

The city’s government in August upgraded its forecast for GDP growth in 2026 to 3.5% to 4.5%, from 2.5% to 3.5% predicted in May.

Financial Secretary Paul Chan said over the weekend that economic growth remained robust in the third quarter as investment continued to surge, adding that the official full-year projection may be revised upward again.

Beijing has signalled its strong backing for the Asian financial hub, with Vice-Premier He Lifeng saying on Nov 3 that developing the city “remains a key strategy for China”.

The national government will continue to endorse a free and open economic environment in Hong Kong, He said in a video speech to the Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in the city. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Asia’s factories lose steam as AI glow meets war’s economic chill
data.description:
TOKYO – Factory activity across Asia continued to expand in October, but growth slowed in major chip exporters, private surveys showed on Nov 2, suggesting the AI boom may be losing momentum as markets start to question the sector’s profitability.

The data points to growing strains on export-led economies, as prolonged conflict in the Middle East keeps fuel and food prices elevated, hitting consumption and business confidence, even as demand for chips and AI-related goods remains resilient.

Manufacturing activity slowed in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, the surveys showed, indicating the drag from the US-Israeli war on Iran may be offsetting the benefits from robust global demand for chips and AI-related goods.

“Strong chip and AI demand had masked soft spots in Asian and global economies. But that’s becoming hard to sustain with the Middle East war dragging on for so long, pushing up fuel and food prices,” said Toru Nishihama, chief emerging market economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute in Tokyo.

“High inflation is hurting Asian consumption. Intensifying price competition from China is also weighing on rival exporters like Japan and South Korea,” he said.

The RatingDog China general manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI), compiled by S&P Global, stood at 52 in October, exceeding the 50-mark that separates growth from contraction but falling from 52.1 in September.

The reading followed official data released on Oct 31 showing China’s factory activity shrank in October, marking the third contraction in four months.

“The PMIs suggest that China’s economic activity lost momentum in October following September’s pick-up. Manufacturing softened a touch, but foreign demand still looks resilient,” said Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics.

“More worrying was the sharp reversal in construction activity and expectations, suggesting that firms have become less confident that fiscal support will provide a substantial boost over the rest of the year.”

AI risks loom

Japan’s PMI eased to 53.3 in October from 54.1 in September, a survey by S&P Global showed, marking the slowest expansion in seven months as output and new orders lost momentum.

South Korea’s factory activity grew in October at the slowest pace in eight months on weaker output and demand, with the PMI falling to 51.3 from 53.9 in September.

Taiwan’s PMI stood at 54.9 in October, down from 56.7 in September. Other countries showed factory activity expanded in October at a faster pace than the previous month, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia.

India’s manufacturing growth slowed in October as domestic demand eased and hiring weakened, though a surge in export orders helped cushion the slowdown.

Asia has outperformed many other regions as manufacturers benefitted from brisk demand for chips and AI-related goods.

But the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Asia’s economic growth to moderate in 2027, and warned of heightening risks from the Iran war-induced energy shock and a potential correction in the AI boom.

The IMF said it now expects Asia’s economy to grow 4.8% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027, higher than projections made in April but still slowing from a 5.0% expansion in 2025.

While Japan has been among the beneficiaries of the AI boom, the central bank warned the technology also poses risks to the country’s long-term economic outlook.

“If growth expectations for AI decline substantially, a tightening of global financial conditions, accompanied by a rapid repricing of stocks and a sharp slowdown in the race for AI development, could significantly hurt Japan’s economy through a plunge in exports and production,” it said. REUTERS

data.title: South Korea exports extend robust growth on AI-fuelled chip boom
data.description:
SEOUL – South Korea’s exports maintained strong growth in October, with an artificial intelligence-driven boom continuing to power the trade-reliant economy.

Exports adjusted for working-day differences climbed 76.1% from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources data released on Nov 1. The value of shipments reached US$115.3 billion (S$147 billion), following the previous month’s record US$121.1 billion. 

On an unadjusted basis, exports rose 93.7%, while imports increased 36%, resulting in a trade surplus of US$42.5 billion. That compared with a revised 83.7% export increase in September.

The continued strength adds to the case for the Bank of Korea (BOK) to raise interest rates in November after policymakers stood pat in October to assess the impact of consecutive increases in July and August. Inflation data due on Nov 3 will provide another key input before the BOK’s decision on Nov 26.

Semiconductors continued to be the main driver of the gains, with chip exports surging 259% from a year earlier to US$56.4 billion. Shipments of computers rose 497%, while petroleum products and cars gained 80%, and 18%, respectively. 

Calendar effects may have complicated the comparisons. The Chuseok holidays fell in September 2026 and October 2025, making working day-adjusted figures a useful gauge of underlying trade momentum. 

The export boom is also putting South Korea on course to exceed US$1 trillion in annual shipments for the first time in 2026, BOK Governor Shin Hyun-song said. That would make it the fourth economy to reach the milestone after the United States, China and Germany, according to the trade ministry.

The figures suggest South Korea’s export engine remained strong at the start of the fourth quarter, even as the benefits of the chip boom have yet to spread evenly across the economy. That divergence complicates the BOK’s task as it weighs strong growth and above-target inflation against weak household demand.

The economy expanded 1% in the third quarter from the previous three months, beating economists’ forecasts for a 0.8% gain. Facility investment jumped 4.1%, but private consumption fell 0.2%, underscoring the uneven benefits of the semiconductor boom.

The BOK expects growth in 2026 and 2027 to substantially exceed its August projections of 3.3% and 2.9%, respectively. It has pointed to continued strength in semiconductor exports and investment, while expecting improving incomes to gradually support a broader consumption recovery.

Governor Shin said monetary policy will remain restrictive until officials are confident inflation will converge to the bank’s 2% target. The BOK will also release updated growth and inflation forecasts with its November rate decision.

Inflation remains a constraint on policymakers even as household demand struggles. Consumer prices rose 2.9% in September from a year earlier, while core inflation excluding food and energy registered 2.8%. Both eased from August but remained well above the BOK’s target.

The won’s appreciation has helped curb imported inflation. Continued export strength and large trade surpluses could support further currency gains, although the pace of any appreciation will also depend on capital flows and global market conditions. Bloomberg

data.title: Big Oil scores US$56b windfall on war-driven refining spike
data.description:
NEW YORK – Big Oil reaped more than US$50 billion (S$64 billion) in windfall profits as conflicts in the Persian Gulf and Russia roiled energy markets and drove refining results to record highs.

ExxonMobil Holdings, Chevron, BP, Shell and TotalEnergies all surpassed third-quarter expectations with combined adjusted net income of US$56.3 billion, driven by an unprecedented fuel-supply crisis that drove pump prices to record highs.

Motorists’ pain at the pump is providing outsized profits for oil supermajors while fanning discontent as US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party head into midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

American voters consistently cite the cost of living as a top concern, with high fuel prices turning traditional Republican strongholds including Texas, Kansas and Alaska into battleground states.

International oil prices are up almost 60% since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, and refining has emerged as an additional chokepoint in the global energy supply chain.

The fighting in the Middle East and Ukrainian strikes in Russia have sidelined about 10% of the world’s fuel-making capacity, handing enormous profits to plants that remain operational.

ExxonMobil’s refining division earned a record US$9.05 billion during the third quarter, almost five times higher than a year earlier, according to a statement on Oct 30. Meanwhile, Chevron’s refineries raked in US$4.93 billion in profit, the highest on record and four times more than a year ago.

For BP, more than half its US$8.46 billion in adjusted net income came from the unit that includes oil refining and trading. Earlier in the week, Shell and Total also disclosed blockbuster results.

ExxonMobil shares rose 1.6% before the start of regular trading in New York. Chevron rose 1.3%. BP climbed as much as 1.8% in London. Shell and Total also rose.

Trump has batted away concerns over petrol and diesel prices, which are higher on average during his second term than under his predecessor, Joe Biden, saying they will come down “very soon” at a rally in Texas this week.

A few days earlier, he praised US oil companies for making “a freaking fortune” for the country, an apparent U-turn after criticising them for “making too much money” this summer.

More volatility ahead

Yet, with the Iran conflict entering its ninth month, the disruptions to global energy markets show little sign of easing despite more ships now passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Until now, markets have leaned heavily on supplies from strategic and commercial stockpiles. But with these buffers running low, price volatility is forecast to escalate.

ExxonMobil, which operates the largest refining system outside China, reported its fourth-highest overall profit in the company’s 156-year history. The company’s adjusted third-quarter earnings of US$4.23 a share were 10 US cents higher than the average analyst estimate.

ExxonMobil raised dividends for the 44th consecutive year, and pledged to maintain US$20 billion in annual buybacks.

Chief financial officer Neil Hansen said the profit surge was less a windfall than a reward for ramping up production at a time when it is most needed. ExxonMobil has increased Gulf Coast distillate production 40% since 2019 as a result of heavy investment since 2020, when rivals sold off fuel-making facilities or converted them to biofuel plants.

“The most meaningful response to those higher global commodity prices that we can offer as a company is to pull every lever that’s available to us to increase supply,” Hansen said during an interview.

ExxonMobil is “putting more diesel on the market in a very strained environment today”.

Chevron also notched its fourth-highest quarterly profit in company history. Its third-quarter net income of US$5.28 a share was 35 US cents higher than the average analyst estimate.

The company maintained share buybacks at US$2.5 billion for the quarter, the low end of its full-year guidance range. For the second consecutive quarter, Chevron executives funnelled windfall profits primarily into debt reduction.

“We don’t react to upside or downside, we don’t move things around,” chief financial officer Eimear Bonner said during an interview. “For now, we’re sticking with our longstanding financial priorities and we’re not making any changes.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Warsh’s ‘forward silence’ risks bigger Treasury market swings, say experts
data.description:
Investors are worried that Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh’s plan to reduce the number of interest-rate decisions each year could be a recipe for more volatility in the US$32 trillion Treasury market. 

Announced by Warsh after the Fed left rates unchanged at the Oct 28 policy meeting, the plan would phase in a shift to six rate decisions a year from eight, with the remaining two gatherings reserved for broader strategic discussions. The move, which would cut the number of decisions down to seven next year, is intended to give officials “time and space” for deliberations, he said.

To traders, however, it adds to a broader shift under Warsh toward a less predictable Fed, including his retreat from forward guidance – essentially telegraphing policy moves – that could increase market turbulence over time.

Bigger gaps between decisions could mean the Fed will need to occasionally deliver larger rate cuts or increases, they said. The shift also raises the likelihood of emergency action between scheduled meetings, potentially fuelling bigger swings in short-dated notes and boosting the premium investors demand to hold longer-term debt.

“This is the clearest signal yet that his Fed has no interest in being a vol suppressor in rates, and is perfectly willing to add to volatility with surprise announcements if conditions warrant,” said Isaac Wheeler, managing director of balance sheet strategy at Derivative Path.

Fewer policy decisions could also reduce opportunities for the Fed to tighten monetary policy in the current cycle, during which it is expected to continue raising rates in order to stave off inflation. That is bullish for shorter term yields on the whole, even as policy uncertainty threatens to lift longer term rates, traders said.

The announcement, coupled with Warsh’s dovish tone at the press conference, helped drive a rally in shorter-dated Treasuries on Oct 28. Longer maturities underperformed, steepening the yield curve. Thirty-year yields have risen about 10 basis points relative to two-year yields since Oct 28. 

Over the long term, “you’re building more risk premium into the curve because you inject these volatility episodes,” said Scott DiMaggio, head of fixed income at AllianceBernstein. 

Regime change

Warsh has suggested that forward guidance limits the Fed’s flexibility and should be reserved only for times of economic crisis.

He has promised to bring “regime change” since taking office in May, and commissioned a task force to examine the US central bank’s communication strategy, including the press conference schedule and the dot-plot of officials’ policy projections.

Warsh first raised the idea of reducing the number of policy decisions at the Fed’s July meeting. On Oct 28, he said the change would allow policymakers to think “anew about big questions”. 

The Oct 28 announcement “marks the start of a new era of ‘forward silence’ at the Fed, and further changes to Fed communications,” said Kerry Craig, global market strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management in Melbourne. 

For now, measures that gauge rate volatility over a two-year horizon have barely moved, in part because details of the new schedule remain scarce, traders said.

The Fed has yet to say which 2027 meeting will be converted into a strategy discussion, beyond indicating it will be in the fall. Traders and economists say the October meeting, which does not include quarterly economic projections, is the most likely candidate.

The immediate impact may also be limited because most market participants are betting the Fed will be done hiking rates a year from now. Overnight-indexed swaps are broadly flat between the September and December meetings, suggesting little disruption if October is dropped as a decision date.

Still, investors say the longer-term consequences of combining fewer rate decisions with less Fed guidance could be far-reaching.

“Fewer decision meetings plus no forward guidance are a recipe for bigger repricing around each one, and more volatility around rates than markets are currently pricing,” said Ali Hassan, portfolio manager at Thornburg Investment Management. BLOOMBERG

data.title: US economy powers ahead as AI boom, shoppers defy oil shock
data.description:
WASHINGTON – The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment more than offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.

Gross domestic product (GDP), the broadest measure of goods and services produced in the country, increased at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, adjusted for inflation, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said on Oct 29.

That was an acceleration from the 2.2% rate in the second quarter, and was the fastest growth in a year.

The strength in growth is in stark contrast to households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.

The report was published less than a week before the midterm elections on Nov 3, which will determine control of Congress.

Polls consistently show that Americans are frustrated with the high cost of living and hold Trump and congressional Republicans responsible for failing to deliver on their promises to improve affordability.

Those frustrations are grounded in reality. Consumer prices were up 3.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, driven in part by high gas prices that are the direct result of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran.

Still, the data released on Oct 29, which is preliminary, is the latest evidence that while Americans may be unhappy about inflation, they have not started to pull back their spending.

That has helped keep the economy on track through a tumultuous period, but it could also be contributing to inflation by making it easier for businesses to pass on price increases to customers.

“This is a hot economy,” said Aditya Bhave, head of US economics for Bank of America. “That’s the good news. The bad news is that inflation is the price we pay for that hot economy, and inflation is going to remain elevated.”

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%.

The US central bank on Oct 28 left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75% to 4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.

Economists expected the Fed to raise rates in December.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters “economic activity is expanding at a strong pace”, noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient”.

Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy.

Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over ​the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending.

Still, economists did expect this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.

Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter.

Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation.

But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above US$4 a gallon as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on, economists anticipated a slowdown in consumer spending. REUTERS

data.title: US Fed leaves rates unchanged as it awaits ‘accumulation of more information’
data.description:
WASHINGTON - The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Oct 28, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections and awaiting further data on the path of inflation.

In a 10-2 decision, the US central bank said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75% to 4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated,” upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation.

“The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2% goal,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. “The Committee will deliver price stability.”

Fed governor Lisa Cook, currently targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, cast her first dissent on a central bank policy decision, favouring a quarter-percentage-point rate hike.

Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice, also dissented in favour of the same rate increase.

The Fed’s latest policy statement is a notable change from the Sept 15-16 meeting, with a hint of the sort of forward guidance Fed chairman Kevin Warsh has said he wants to avoid.

The central bank’s assessment of the economy was upgraded to “strong” from the “solid” expansion seen as of the September meeting, while investment was still described as robust and job gains were viewed as keeping pace with the workforce.

Market reaction was muted, with US stocks paring gains slightly after the decision. US Treasury yields extended their rise, with the 10-year Treasury note yield at 5.028%. Short-term interest-rate futures rose a bit, as traders pulled back a bit on bets of Fed rate hikes ahead.

“A hold isn’t relief,” said Kelly Brown, chief executive officer of deposit management company Ampersand. “It’s the Fed telling Main Street to wait. With inflation still at 3.7%, and oil above US$100 a barrel, businesses can’t count on borrowing costs coming down anytime soon.”

Fears that inflation is broadening

The outcome of this week’s meeting was widely expected after top Fed officials indicated they saw no rush to raise rates again following the quarter-percentage-point increase approved in September, despite inflation data in the meantime that was stronger than forecast and concerns that price pressures are broadening across the economy.

Energy costs remain high, including for diesel fuel, which is a key input for shipping, agriculture, and other industries. Inflation and the cost of living in general have been central to the political races that will determine whether Trump’s Republican Party remains in control of both houses of Congress on Nov 3, or whether Democrats move into leadership positions and gain more robust oversight powers, including over the Fed.

Investors continue to expect further rate hikes will be needed, beginning in December and continuing into 2027, to lower inflation that is currently around a percentage point above the Fed’s target and has shown little progress in recent months.

The US central bank has missed its inflation target for five and a half years, a fact that has left some officials worried that businesses and households are becoming accustomed to faster price increases and may plan for them in ways that will make inflation harder to control. REUTERS

data.title: ‘Don’t panic’: Marcos vows to defend Philippine peso after slide to record low
data.description:
MANILA – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said on Oct 28 the Philippine authorities would extend their defence of the sinking Philippine peso after the currency hit a fresh record low this week.

“We will continue to do all that we can to make sure that the value of the peso does not continue to go down,” Marcos told reporters a day after meeting with central bank and government officials.

“People can take solace in the fact that our policy toward the peso is to continue to defend the peso as hard as we possibly can,” he said.

The Philippine authorities have taken a number of measures to address the impact of a weak currency.

The central bank has raised its key interest rate four times, including a jumbo 50-basis-point hike in September, while Marcos and central bank Governor Eli Remolona have both announced support for the currency.

The nation has also deployed some of its foreign reserves to limit the peso’s decline.

Despite these efforts, the peso has dropped more than 8% against the US dollar, and sank to its most recent record low of 64.20 per US dollar on Oct 27. The currency gained 0.2% on Oct 28 to 64.025.

“Don’t panic,” Marcos told reporters. The currency’s weakness “is an effect of rising prices of oil, and consequently the rising prices of fuel, and its effect on the economy”, he said.

The president’s comments contrast with those he made in March, when he said there were limits to how far the authorities could defend the peso as market forces pushed the US dollar higher.

The president’s more supportive stance may help improve sentiment toward the peso, but it is unlikely to be enough to stem the currency’s weakness, said Jonathan Ravelas, a senior adviser at Reyes Tacandong & Company.

“As long as there is uncertainty arising from the Middle East crisis, the peso will remain under pressure,” he said. “Hopefully, remittances and another 50-basis-point hike by the central bank could slow down the peso’s depreciation.”

Addressing the impact of a weak currency would require both monetary and non-monetary measures in a country that imports nearly all of its oil requirements, and may include more energy-saving steps similar to those implemented in March, Ravelas said.

The government said this week it will provide subsidies and other measures to help its citizens cope with the impact of the El Niño weather pattern and the conflict in the Middle East. These include a price freeze on basic goods until end-2026.

“Inflation is coming from the supply side,” Marcos said. “So monetary measures can only go so far. We have to find other ways” such as working to bring down food prices, he said. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Singapore unveils new initiatives to help companies harness AI, such as to develop new products
data.description:
SINGAPORE - Singapore launched three new initiatives to support companies of all sizes in boosting their capability to implement and scale artificial intelligence (AI) and use the technology to transform their businesses.

The initiatives reflect Singapore’s recognition that AI will rapidly become the defining force behind the next wave of innovation, transforming how new ideas, products and services are developed and commercialised.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong announced the initiatives at the Singapore Week of Innovation and Technology (SWITCH) 2026 on Oct 27, noting that Singapore will explore ways to make AI work better for its industries and workers, to build an economy that is more innovative, competitive and inclusive.

“AI offers opportunities to raise productivity, and develop new products and capabilities,” he said in his speech at the event’s opening ceremony held at Marina Bay Sands.

The initiatives follow the four national AI missions - advanced manufacturing, finance, healthcare and connectivity - announced by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong during Budget 2026.

Led by Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) in partnership with other Government agencies, the new initiatives include a Champions of AI programme to help ambitious Singapore-based companies committed to making AI a core driver of growth.

Dubbed by EnterpriseSG as the national flagship AI initiative, the programme will begin with a cohort of 24 companies across various industries, with more companies progressively coming on board.

The list of champions includes well-known local names such as DBS, OCBC, UOB, ST Engineering, Seatrium, PSA International, Singapore Airlines, Singtel Singapore, Keppel and Sembcorp.

The agency will work closely with these companies to develop tailored, long-term AI transformation roadmaps and provide them with access to curated AI expertise and solution providers, supporting enterprise-wide deployment of AI and change management, as well as workforce redesign and upskilling.

The second initiative is a series of agentic AI workshops to provide hands-on guidance to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) for adopting and scaling AI solutions, and catalytic AI solutions workshops that will advance sector-wide AI adoption, starting with the advanced manufacturing, trade and logistics sectors.

Agentic AI is an artificial intelligence system that can accomplish a specific goal with limited supervision. It consists of AI agents—machine learning models that mimic human decision-making to solve problems in real time. 

The workshops will enable micro-entrepreneurs and small business owners to start their AI journey, identify practical use cases and build working prototypes tailored to their own businesses.

In the pilot run of the initiative, more than 280 small businesses were supported to apply agentic AI tools in areas such as marketing, sales and customer service.

More workshops will be rolled out next month and scaled further in 2027.

EnterpriseSG said feedback from workshop participants showed that many businesses today are experimenting with AI but lack in-house tech capabilities and bandwidth to refine, integrate and deploy these solutions to meet their operational needs.

The agency will look into providing support to companies for last-mile AI deployment.

Perhaps the most ambitious of the three initiatives is MARVEL-AI, which stands for Accelerating Advanced Materials Innovation through AI and Automation.

Advanced materials are substances intentionally engineered, modified, or synthesised to exhibit novel or significantly enhanced physical and chemical properties. They deliver superior performance, structural strength, durability, and sustainability compared to traditional metals, ceramics or polymers.

These engineered materials act as the baseline enabling agents for industries - such as semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, energy and chemicals - allowing breakthroughs that are physically impossible with conventional inputs.

While newer materials can unlock better products, each material candidate has to go through a lengthy R&D process - experimentation, characterisation, validation, process development and industrial translation.

This can involve multiple development cycles, substantial resources and separate hand-offs between research and downstream development.

Hence, MARVEL-AI is designed to change the speed and scale of materials innovation, with a differentiated proposition that connects AI-enabled materials discovery, experimentation and validation with the pathway towards real-world industrial applications.

The initiative is likely to put Singapore on the map of advanced materials’ innovation - an area of intense competition among a handful of countries including the US, China, Japan and South Korea, the UK and Switzerland.

Led by the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*Star), the initiative is supported by the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, EnterpriseSG, Singapore Economic Development Board and National Research Foundation.

The initiative received initial funding of S$150 million from the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 (RIE2030) - Singapore’s 5-year S$37 billion science and innovation master plan announced last year.

MARVEL-AI is focused on four materials classes: metal alloys, polymers and organics, ceramics, and composites.

It also aims to create high-value startups, anchor large multinationals with materials development mandates, and uplift local enterprises with frontier technologies.

Gan, who is also the Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), said AI models such as Google’s Project GNoME (Graph Networks for Materials Exploration) and Microsoft’s MatterGen have shown the potential of AI to accelerate materials discovery.

He said the AI models will identify promising materials and design experiments, while the highly automated A*Star laboratories will rapidly synthesise and test them.

“This will create opportunities for industry partnerships, enterprise growth and new ventures. We will also develop talent with capabilities spanning materials science, AI and automation, creating good job opportunities.

“Together, these efforts can deepen our industrial capabilities, develop new sources of growth, and strengthen Singapore’s position in advanced materials innovation,” he said.

data.title: Singapore factory output growth slows to 3.4% in September as pharmaceutical production fell
data.description:
SINGAPORE - Singapore’s manufacturing output grew at a slower pace in September, weighed down by a sharp contraction in pharmaceutical production, even as demand for artificial intelligence-related products continued to support the electronics and precision engineering sectors.

Factory output rose 3.4% year on year in September, easing from the 15.4% expansion recorded in August, according to data released by the Economic Development Board (EDB) on Oct 26.

The number was far below the 7.1% forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll.

Biomedical manufacturing output plunged 32.8% in September. The decline was driven largely by the pharmaceuticals segment, where output contracted 65.9%.

The medical technology segment also recorded a 1.7% decline amid softer export demand.

The precision engineering cluster recorded the largest growth in September with output rising 31%, supported by the higher production of semiconductor equipment in the machinery and systems segment, which saw 34.8% growth.

The precision modules and components segment also recorded 12.4% growth with higher output of industrial rubber goods, precision metal products and dies, moulds, tools, jigs and fixtures.

Robust AI-related demand drove a 5.7% growth in the electronics cluster with most segments expanding, though September’s expansion was far lower than August’s 28.3%.

The infocomms and consumer electronics, and computer peripherals and data storage segments saw the largest expansions at 29% and 21.3% respectively, while semiconductors output slowed down to just 1.9% growth, compared to 25.9% in August.

The other electronic modules and components segment contracted by 4.2%.

The transport engineering cluster grew 10.6%, with the land segment recording the largest growth at 31.4%. The aerospace segment also grew 16.3%, supported by higher production of aircraft parts and sustained maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) jobs from commercial airlines.

This growth was partially offset by lower shipyard activity and lower production of oil and gas field equipment in the marine and offshore engineering segment, which contracted 6.3%.

The general manufacturing industries cluster grew 4%. The food, beverages and tobacco segment saw output rise 11% due to higher production of beverage and dairy products , while an increase in commercial printing drove the printing segment to expand by 7.6%. The miscellaneous segment contracted 8.4% however, as it recorded lower production of structural metal products and furniture.

Biomedical manufacturing saw the greatest contraction at 32.8%, led by the pharmaceuticals segment’s 65.9% due to a different mix of active pharmaceutical ingredients being produced, much worse than August’s 4% decline. The medical technology segment also fell 1.7% due to softer export demand, after seeing growth over the last three months.

The chemicals cluster declined 4.6%. The other chemicals segment contracted 19.4% due to lower output of fragrances and softer demand, while the petrochemicals segment saw a decline of 24.3%, as production remained constrained by softer demand and feedstock supply disruptions.

In contrast, the specialties and petroleum segments recorded output growth of 14.3% and 4.6% respectively, with the former producing more industrial gases, chemicals and mineral oil additives.

data.title: Singapore’s core inflation eases to 2% in September
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore’s core inflation dropped in September, due to lower core inflation and private transport inflation.

Core inflation – which excludes private transport and accommodation to better reflect household expenses – eased to 2%, down from 2.2% in August, according to data from the Singapore Department of Statistics on October 23.

Overall inflation fell to 2.2% in September from 2.3% in the previous month owing to lower inflation in services, retail and other goods, and private transport.

Private transport inflation slowed to 7.1%, down from 7.5% in August and 8% in July, due to a more gradual increase in car prices.

Meanwhile, accommodation inflation went up to 0.9% in September from August’s 0.8% as housing rents increased at a faster pace.

Services inflation dropped to 1.7%, from 2% in August, due to a smaller increase in point-to-point transport service costs and a larger decline in telecommunication service prices.

Retail and other goods inflation dropped to 1.2% in September from the previous months’ 1.8%, as furniture prices declined and clothing prices rose at a slower pace.

Food inflation increased slightly to 2.4%, from 2.3% in August and from 2.2% in July, due to higher inflation in both non-cooked food and food services.

Electricity and gas prices inflation remained unchanged at 8.7% for September, as electricity prices rose at a similar pace as in August.

data.title: Philippines surprises with jumbo hike as inflation surges, peso slumps
data.description:
MANILA – The Philippine central bank delivered an outsized interest-rate hike and signalled readiness to tighten further to rein in resurgent inflation and support a peso that has sunk to a record low.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) increased on Oct 22 the target reverse repurchase rate by a half-point to 5.5% as expected by only one of 25 economists in a Bloomberg News survey. Twenty-four predicted a less aggressive, quarter-point hike.

Broadening price pressures and upside risks to inflation requires a “strong” response, the BSP said in its statement. “Such a decisive response will make monetary policy appropriately restrictive. This will contain second-round effects and firmly anchor inflation expectations.”

“The BSP stands ready to take further monetary policy action as necessary to ensure the timely return of inflation to the target,” it added.

The nation’s benchmark stock index ended 0.7% lower after the decision, snapping five straight days of gains. The Philippine peso continued its decline on Oct 22.

The move underlines how drastically the inflation threat has built up for the Philippines, which must now confront the possibility of a severe El Nino dry spell, while still reeling from the impact of the global oil shock.

The Philippine peso also hit a fresh historic low on Oct 22 after breaching the key psychological level of 63 per US dollar for the first time last week. The weakened currency risks fanning inflation as the nation relies heavily on imports for fuel and food supplies.

The monetary authority has now increased borrowing costs by a total of 125 basis points since the Iran war broke out early in 2026, even as the Philippine economy is growing at its slowest pace since the pandemic. Still, the inflation outlook has hardly improved.

The BSP kept its forecast for 6.1% inflation in 2026, while significantly raising its estimate for 2027 to 6% from 5.4% previously. The gauge is only seen to moderate to 3.3% in 2028.

“The forecasts were worse than we thought,” Governor Eli Remolona said in a news briefing after the decision. “There was a bit of a sense of urgency to try and dampen these inflationary pressures.”

Price pressures are building up as renewed fighting in the Middle East drives up global oil prices, while transport fares have been raised. The biggest risk ahead is a possible severe El Nino dry spell that could hit farm production, according to the governor.

Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr, who was the only one to correctly predict the decision, said the jumbo rate hike reinforces the BSP’s inflation-fighting credentials.

Consumer prices already surged 7.2% in September from a year earlier, reversing four months of deceleration. That brought the year-to-date inflation average to 5.4%, well above the central bank’s 3% target.

The governor expressed concern about peso weakness and its impact on imported inflation, even as he said the BSP would not deplete its reserves to defend a specific level of the currency.

He added that domestic economic activity should recover by the first quarter of 2027, supported by improved government spending.

While the central bank has left the door open for more rate hikes, Pantheon Macroeconomics’ Miguel Chanco said further tightening is not a done deal for the BSP’s December meeting.

“Incidentally, today’s larger-than-expected adjustment could’ve been motivated as a front-loading of what would’ve been another uncontroversial 25-basis point hike in the last sit-down of this year,” Chanco said. BLOOMBERG

data.title: S’pore GDP grew by 5.4% in third quarter of 2026
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore’s economy grew by 5.4% in the third quarter, moderating from 6.2% in the previous quarter.

On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally-adjusted basis, the economy expanded by 1.1 per cent, easing from the 1.5% growth in the second quarter.

The manufacturing sector grew by 7.5% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, slower than the 12.9% growth in the previous quarter.

The construction sector expanded by 8.8% year-on-year in the third quarter, faster than the 6.1% growth in the preceding quarter, as both public and private sector construction output increased.

Among the services sectors, the wholesale & retail trade and transportation & storage

sectors collectively grew by 8% year-on-year in the third quarter, extending the 6.9% growth in the previous quarter. All sectors within the group expanded during the quarter, except for the retail trade sector.

data.title: Record imports push US trade balance deep into the red in August
data.description:
WASHINGTON – The US trade deficit widened more than expected in August as imports jumped to a record high against the backdrop of robust domestic demand, keeping trade on track to again subtract from economic growth in the third quarter.

The deterioration reported by the Commerce Department on Oct 6 was despite President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariffs on imports, which he has argued are meant to shrink the trade gap.

The US posted record goods trade deficits with at least three countries, including Mexico.

Economists have long argued that the US does not have the capacity to produce enough goods to meet its consumption needs.

“The administration’s trade policies have largely been a failure. Trade tariffs have done nothing to reduce America’s reliance on the import of foreign-produced goods,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS.

“The cost of American labour is simply too high to produce goods here cheap enough for consumers to even think about purchasing. Even if US manufacturers were willing, the factories could not be built here fast enough to produce the goods that consumers depend on,” he said.

The trade shortfall increased 13.7% to US$105.6 billion (S$135 billion), the largest since March 2025, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis and Census Bureau said. Economists polled by Reuters expected the deficit to be US$102 billion.

The trade deficit was at US$79.8 billion when Trump was elected for a second term in November 2024. August’s deterioration was flagged by data that showed an import-driven surge in the goods trade deficit.

Domestic demand increased at its fastest pace in more than 3½ years in the second quarter, reflecting robust consumer spending and business spending on equipment, mostly related to AI.

The trend appears to have spilled over into the third quarter, with data in September showing strong consumer spending in August, as well as orders and shipments of non-defence capital goods, excluding aircraft.

But businesses are relying on imports to meet demand.

Imports increased 4.3% to an all-time high of US$420.8 billion in August. Goods imports jumped 5.3% to US$342.2 billion. They were boosted by a US$9.1 billion increase in industrial supplies and materials, which include petroleum.

Crude oil imports rose US$3.3 billion, while non-monetary gold increased US$3.1 billion. Non-monetary gold is excluded in the calculation of gross domestic product (GDP).

Capital goods imports soared US$6.2 billion to a record high US$146.4 billion, driven by semiconductors and other industrial machinery. But imports of computer accessories decreased US$1.6 billion.

Trade set to weigh on growth

Exports rose 1.4% to US$315.2 billion. Goods exports increased 2.2% to US$205.7 billion, reflecting a US$6.3 billion rise in industrial supplies and materials, mostly non-monetary gold, crude oil and fuel oil.

Capital goods exports rose by US$1.3 billion, lifted by semiconductors and computers. But exports of civilian aircraft fell by US$1 billion.

Consumer goods exports dropped US$2.2 billion, pulled down by a US$2.4 billion decline in pharmaceutical preparations.

The goods trade deficit increased 10.3% to US$136.6 billion in August. When adjusted for inflation, it widened US$8.7 billion, or 8.2%, to US$114.7 billion.

Trade has subtracted from GDP for three straight quarters, and economists estimate it could cut as much as 2.5 percentage points from GDP in the third quarter.

Growth estimates for the July-September quarter are mostly above a 3% annualised rate, with consumer spending expected to offset the drag from imports. The US economy grew at a 2.2% pace in the second quarter.

Services imports rose less than US$100 million to US$78.5 billion in August, amid a small gain in transport. Charges for the use of intellectual property fell as did travel.

Exports of services also advanced by less than US$100 million to US$109.5 billion. There were modest increases in charges for the use of intellectual property and other business services. Travel and financial services both declined.

The US had record goods trade shortfalls with Mexico, Vietnam and Malaysia. It maintained deficits with Taiwan, China, the European Union, South Korea, Canada and India among other trade partners.

The country, however, posted a record goods trade surplus with Belgium, while maintaining surpluses with the Netherlands, South and Central America, Britain, Hong Kong, Brazil, Australia and Saudi Arabia. REUTERS

data.title: IMF warns cost-of-living shocks cause ‘lasting deterioration’ in affordability
data.description:
WASHINGTON – The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned on Oct 6 that price increases for necessities like food and energy, fuelled by the wars in Iran and Ukraine, are more persistent than previously expected.

Global prices for many commodities have remained elevated for several years, fuelled first by pandemic supply chain shortages and then by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

The war in Ukraine snarled supply chains for many food-related goods as well as energy, and the US-Israel war on Iran has seen energy and fertilizer prices skyrocket due to the closure of a key Gulf supply route.

“We find that the prices of necessities relative to other goods continue rising for more than a year after the start of a typical episode, and remain persistently elevated,” the IMF said in a blog post accompanying its new report.

“As a result, people face not only a temporary spike in food and energy costs, but a lasting deterioration in the affordability of essentials relative to other items,” it said.

Households worldwide have struggled with cost-of-living increases due to the wars and the pandemic, with wages struggling to keep up with persistent price pressures.

The Iran war, launched in February 2026, has pushed global inflation and saw the IMF upgrade its forecast for the metric to 4.7% worldwide in 2026, compared to 4.1% the year before.

The IMF is due to release the main portion of its World Economic Outlook update next week, with new figures for global growth and inflation forecasts.

The latest report is part of that release, focusing on lessons learned from the cost-of-living crises of the last five years.

The IMF warned that the consequences of so-called supply shocks extended far beyond “a few months of higher inflation”.

Central banks across the world have begun raising interest rates to combat inflation.

Raising the key rate of an economy can help fight higher prices, but also tends to slow economic activity, a difficult balancing act in developing countries that may not be able to afford the slowdown.

The report said the persistent inflationary pressures were a threat to macroeconomic stability for many countries.

“Inflation remains elevated long after the initial surge in food and energy prices,” it said. “Inflation expectations also rise and stay above pre-crisis levels for years, suggesting that these episodes may complicate efforts by central banks to control inflation.”

The burden of those price increases falls disproportionately on working-class families, for whom spending on necessities is both non-negotiable and forms a larger share of their monthly spending.

As a result, such inflation has a “substantial” impact on increasing poverty and income inequality.

The IMF called on countries to avoid broad-based subsidies to combat such crises, and to instead issue “targeted and temporary transfers” to those who need them most.

With global debt levels at elevated levels, however, many low-income and developing countries lack the fiscal space to do so, especially given the repeated shocks since the pandemic. AFP

data.title: Bank of Japan says AI boom may have eased financial conditions, warns of market risks
data.description:
TOKYO - Bank of Japan (BOJ) Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida said the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom may have eased financial conditions by stoking demand and boosting asset prices, but warned of the risk of a market pullback if expected profits fail to materialise.

“It is a big positive demand shock, which has put upward pressure on the economy and prices,” Uchida said on worldwide AI adoption in the text of a speech on the central bank’s website on Oct 5.

The technology could also raise productivity and enhance capital stock accumulation, which in turn might affect a country’s natural rate of interest, he said.

“Tentatively, it appears the demand side has come first and made financial conditions more accommodative on balance,” Uchida said. “But there is a risk of correction if profits do not follow.”

While AI has boosted stock prices and made financial conditions easier, huge bond issuance by AI-related firms has put upward pressure on long-term interest rates, Uchida said.

The BOJ will continue to carefully examine economic and financial data to ascertain a “consistent picture” on AI’s impact, he said, adding that the overall effect on Japan’s natural rate of interest was still hard to gauge.

The BOJ has identified robust AI-related demand as among factors that could push underlying inflation above its 2% target, necessitating further monetary tightening.

The central bank raised interest rates in June and September as the energy shock caused by the Iran war added to price pressures from a weak yen, which increases import costs.

Japan imports almost all of its crude oil, of which most came from the Middle East before the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. REUTERS

data.title: Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cuts oil prices to Asia
data.description:
Saudi Arabia has unexpectedly cut November crude oil prices for Asia while it raised those for north-west Europe and the Mediterranean regions, a pricing document showed on Oct 5.

The largest Middle Eastern crude exporter set the November Arab Light crude oil official selling price to Asia at US$5 a barrel below the average of Oman and Dubai prices, down US$3 from the previous month.

The discount for November is the widest since June 2020, Reuters data showed.

This was against expectations of a US$3 a barrel hike for its November OSP in a Reuters survey in line with gains seen in the Middle Eastern benchmarks.

State oil company Saudi Aramco made deeper cuts of US$5 a barrel for the November OSPs of heavier grades – Arab Medium and Arab Heavy – sold to Asia.

Aramco has been looking at offering discounts for oil loaded off Oman to compensate buyers for record freight rates, people familiar with the matter said last week, as it sought to protect its market share after the regional conflict hit exports.

Separately, Saudi Aramco raised the November OSPs for north-west Europe by US$3 a barrel across all grades after it resumed exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

Aramco kept prices unchanged for buyers in the United States.

Saudi Arabia and other members of OPEC+ agreed on Oct 4 to keep oil production targets steady for November, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year. REUTERS

data.title: US to unveil measures against excess manufacturing in ‘weeks’: Nikkei report
data.description:
SINGAPORE - US President Donald Trump’s administration will act soon, most probably with a harsh trade tariff, against trading partners allegedly producing more goods than they can consume domestically.

US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer told Japanese news outlet Nikkei Asia: “If you’re a country that doesn’t take action to stop the effects of excess capacity... whether it’s in your country or coming from a third country, I’m not going to sit there and take it.”

“The United States is going to act,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of the G20 (Group of Twenty) meeting in the US city of Milwaukee.

Greer said the US will announce countermeasures within “weeks” against overproduction that displaces existing US domestic production or prevents investment and expansion in the US manufacturing sector.

The USTR launched an investigation in March against 16 economies, including Singapore, under Section 301 of the Trade Act focused on alleged excess manufacturing capacity.

Other economies subject to the inquiry include some of the US’ largest trading partners: China, the European Union, Mexico, India, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Cambodia, Vietnam and Bangladesh are also part of the investigation.

A new tariff will add to the 12.5 per cent levy Singapore became subject to in July following a USTR scrutiny into 60 US trading partners regarding their alleged failure to enforce prohibitions on imports made with forced labour.

Separately, US sectoral tariffs - with rates ranging from 25 per cent to 50 per cent - on steel, aluminium, copper and automotive parts also apply to some Singapore exports. Singapore may also face a possible US tariff on its semiconductor exports.

In the interview with Nikkei, Greer cited intense competition, or involution, in China’s electric vehicle market as an example of excess production that squeezes profit margins.

You can see “the Chinese on their own independently acknowledging to some degree that excess capacity exists,” Greer said. “They call the effects of it involution, but it’s rooted in excess capacity”.

Greer also referred to the G20 meeting in Milwaukee, where trade officials from member countries announced an agreement to tackle the global steel glut which many believe stems from state subsidies that encourage excess production of the refined metal.

In an earlier meeting of G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors in Asheville last month, 19 of the 20 members agreed to take action against non-market economic policies, excessive trade surpluses, and an over-reliance on cheap exports.

Greer said that at international forums like the G20, China is “generally defensive about this because they know that they are part of the broader distortion”.

He also called out the policies of China’s neighbours including Japan and Vietnam, which have seen their exports to the US rise in recent years as shipments from China declined.

Vietnam has “no consumption,” Greer told Nikkei. Workers there “can’t buy the things they’re making, so they have to send them to us”.

“They need to increase their domestic demand” through measures including protection of worker rights and higher wages,” he said.

Greer also suggested that Japan has its own overcapacity problem.

“They have zombie firms that should have been bankrupt long ago, but they just ... keep them surviving, whether it’s Japan or other countries,” he said.

In its engagements with Trump administration officials, Singapore has denied that it enjoys a trade surplus with the US or that its exports to the world’s largest economy stem from any form of excess capacity.

In fact, the US has maintained a substantial trade surplus with Singapore for more than two decades. In 2025, that surplus exceeded US$33 billion (S$42 billion), according to the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

Singapore, despite its small size, is the third-largest Asian investor in the US, behind Japan and South Korea. Bilateral trade and Singapore’s investments in the US support around 350,000 American jobs.

About 6,600 American companies are based in Singapore, while more than 250 Singapore companies operate across 45 US states, in sectors ranging from logistics and agribusiness to aerospace and shipbuilding.

data.title: Japan PM vows to underpin yen by boosting economic competitiveness
data.description:
TOKYO - Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the administration’s efforts to boost the country’s economic competitiveness will help ensure market confidence in the yen, according to a recorded interview aired by Nippon Television on Oct 1.

She also said she told United States President Donald Trump that the yen’s undervaluation was a problem when the two met in September.

“Our economic policy is not aimed at manipulating exchange rates,” Takaichi said.

“My administration aims to boost Japan’s growth potential by increasing the economy’s supply capacity through bold investment in crisis management and growth areas,” she said. “Such efforts would strengthen Japan’s global competitiveness, thereby helping ensure market confidence in the yen.”

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also endorsed Japan’s economic policy and made no specific demands when Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama met him for bilateral talks on Aug 31, Takaichi said.

“There’s no change to our stance of pursuing both a strong economy and sustainable fiscal policy,” she said. REUTERS
